summary: Defines an IMAP extension that tells clients the messages on an IMAP server are also available through JMAP, and how to reach them. It helps clients migrate gradually to JMAP or use JMAP extensions inside an IMAP client.

eli5.summary: An old mailbox door now has a sign that says there is a newer door to the same mailbox. This helps apps switch over slowly.

questions: how to find jmap from imap

what does the getjmapaccess command do
subtitle: An IMAP extension that tells a logged-in client the same mail is also reachable through JMAP, and where.

tldr.problem: A mail client talking to an IMAP server has no standard way to learn that the same messages are also available through JMAP, so gradual migration to JMAP is awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises a JMAPACCESS capability after authentication, and the client can send GETJMAPACCESS to receive the URL of the JMAP session resource. Mailbox and message IDs are the same in both protocols.
tldr.outcome: Clients can move to JMAP step by step or use JMAP extensions from inside an IMAP client. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Failure reply
facts.value: Tagged BAD when no JMAP server is known

today: RFC 9698 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why IMAP Needs to Point at JMAP
sections.content:
RFC 9698 defines an IMAP extension called JMAPACCESS. It lets an IMAP server declare that the messages in its mailstore are also available through JMAP, the JSON Meta Application Protocol defined in RFC 8620, and tells the client how to reach them.

The goal is gradual migration. A client can keep using IMAP while it starts using JMAP, or it can use JMAP extensions inside an IMAP client. For simplicity, only complete equivalence is supported: the same set of messages must be available through both protocols.
sections.eli5: Some apps want to move from the old way of reading mail to a newer way, but not all at once. This sign tells them the newer way exists.

sections.title: What the Capability Promises
sections.content:
By advertising the JMAPACCESS capability, the server asserts that if a mailbox or message has a particular object ID in IMAP or JMAP, then the same mailbox or message is accessible through the other protocol with the same ID. The server MUST also advertise the OBJECTID extension from RFC 8474. The JMAP session resource that reaches the same messages is called "the JMAP server" in the text.

Some things are deliberately not promised. Message lifetime is unaffected: a message read through IMAP may be gone half a second later when the client asks JMAP. Servers are encouraged, not required, to report the same flags and other data through both protocols. Mailboxes may have different names in IMAP and JMAP even when they share an ID.

The shared IDs are what make the two views line up: a client can find a message in one protocol and refer to it in the other.
sections.eli5: Every folder and letter has the same name tag on both doors, so you can say which one you mean. But someone might throw a letter away between your two peeks.

sections.title: When the Server Advertises It
sections.content:
The capability depends on how the client logged in. When the server processes LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE and enters Authenticated state, it considers the way the client authenticated. If it can infer that those credentials suffice to authenticate through JMAP, it MUST include JMAPACCESS in any capability list sent after that point, including the list some servers send immediately on success.

The examples in the RFC show the range. With SASL OAuth (RFC 7628), the server knows the OAuth backend is shared with its JMAP side, so the access token works for both. With LOGIN, the capability appears when IMAP and JMAP share a password database. If an operator has disabled passwords for JMAP but still allows them for IMAP, the login succeeds without the capability. If the password is wrong, the server never enters Authenticated state and need not mention JMAPACCESS at all.
sections.eli5: The sign only shows up if your key also opens the new door. If your key only fits the old door, there is no sign.

sections.title: The GETJMAPACCESS Command
sections.content:
The GETJMAPACCESS command asks the server for the session URL of the JMAP server that provides access to the same mail. It is added to the authenticated-state commands.

  • If such a JMAP server is known, the server MUST send an untagged JMAPACCESS response containing the session resource URL as a quoted string, followed by a tagged OK.
  • If none is known, the server MUST send a tagged BAD and MUST NOT include JMAPACCESS in the capability list.

The formal syntax extends RFC 9051 with command-auth =/ "GETJMAPACCESS" and resp-jmapaccess = "JMAPACCESS" SP quoted. The syntax in RFC 3501 is extended similarly, so the extension works with IMAP4rev1 as well as IMAP4rev2.
sections.eli5: You ask, "Where is the new door?" The server answers with the address, or says it does not know of one.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples. In the first, the client authenticates with AUTHENTICATE OAUTHBEARER; the server replies with a capability list containing JMAPACCESS, the client sends GETJMAPACCESS, and the server answers with the JMAP URL and OK. The second does the same after a successful LOGIN. The third shows a successful LOGIN with no capability because the operator disabled passwords for JMAP. The fourth shows a failed LOGIN, which just gets NO.

The RFC notes that real connections use longer capability lists, much longer AUTHENTICATE arguments and TLS; the examples are abbreviated to focus on JMAPACCESS.
sections.eli5: The examples show a few ways of logging in. Sometimes the sign appears, sometimes it does not, and a wrong password gets a plain "no".

sections.title: Internationalized Addresses
sections.content: All JMAP servers support internationalized email addresses (RFC 6530). If the IMAP server does not, or if the IMAP client does not issue ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT (RFC 6855), the client may receive accurate address fields through JMAP and downgraded fields through IMAP. The RFC points to RFC 6857 and RFC 6858 for examples of downgrading, and says that issuing ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT is a simple way to sidestep the issue.
sections.eli5: If the old door cannot show fancy letters in names, the new door may show them correctly. Asking the old door to allow fancy letters fixes the mismatch.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
JMAPACCESS reveals to authenticated IMAP clients that they could authenticate via JMAP with the same credentials, and that object IDs match. Normally nothing is revealed about authentication. The RFC argues this is acceptable: an attacker who sees it already has valid credentials, and Section 2.2 of RFC 8620 tells them how to find the URL without this extension. It concludes the extension does not noticeably help an attacker and that its migration value far outweighs the risk.

IANA added the JMAPACCESS capability to the IMAP Capabilities Registry.
sections.eli5: The sign is only shown to people who already got in with a key, and they could have found the new door anyway, so little is given away.
